prs.title: Fix adjustment layer name clicks targeting masks
prs.body:
Fixes #9694

Clicking an adjustment layer's name now selects its contents instead of its mask, including when that same layer's pixel or vector mask was previously selected. Explicit mask-thumbnail clicks and new-layer creation keep their existing behavior. Fill-layer row targeting and rasterization prompts, and ordinary raster-layer row behavior, are unchanged.

Regression coverage uses actual native UI clicks at 1x and 2x, checks the selected content-thumbnail brackets, and preserves the existing #3369 Properties/creation regression. The new regression fails on the base revision and passes with this fix. An actual Fill-black regression verifies that adjustment content is preserved and only its mask changes. Pixel painting on adjustment layers retains its existing mask fallback.

Validation:
- 29 mask-thumbnail tests pass; independent code review found no blocker.
- Strict all-target UI Clippy, formatting, layering, and WebAssembly checks pass.
- Full UI library run: 4,013 passed, 26 failed, 18 ignored. Integration: 132 passed, 1 failed, 1 ignored. All 27 failures are missing-glyph panics in egui 0.37 with the fonts available in this local build; the full suite is not green. Doctests pass (0 tests).
- Native macOS offscreen screenshots rendered and visually inspected. Windows/Linux UI has not been manually tested.

prs.title: perf(algo): row-parallel local_sharpen with fast-path protect_detail (#5426)
prs.body:
Refs #5426. Follow-up to #5499.

## Problem

#5499 parallelized `local_blur` and the per-dab mix in `DabTool::Focus`, but `local_sharpen` (`crates/algo/src/retouch.rs`) stayed single-threaded. `protect_detail` also recomputed boundary clamping and strided lookups for the 8-neighbour window inside the per-channel loop, for every pixel in the dab. With large brushes (500–2500 px) interactive strokes lagged badly and stalled the application.

## Change

- `local_sharpen` processes window rows in parallel (`out.par_chunks_mut(stride)`), with a `wasm32` serial fallback like `local_blur`.
- `protect_detail` computes the 3×3 neighbourhood offsets once, outside the channel loop.
- Interior pixels (`x > 0 && x + 1 < w && y > 0 && y + 1 < h`) use direct stride offsets and skip boundary clamping, which covers over 99.9% of pixels in large dabs.
- New `retouch_sharpen_exact` integration test compares against the frozen scalar oracle bit for bit across layouts, edges and channels.
- New `bench_sharpen_tool` example, matching `bench_blur_tool`.

## Timings

GitHub Actions `rc-bench`, 4 vCPU AMD EPYC 9V45. Output is bit-identical at every size (fingerprint `96d1f22de93b16ec` at 8-bit, `9282e5cfc9e3ec48` at 16-bit).

| Depth | Brush | Before | After | Less time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8-bit | 100 px | 40.75 ms | 27.37 ms | 33% |
| 8-bit | 500 px | 214.14 ms | 153.37 ms | 28% |
| 8-bit | 1000 px | 738.67 ms | 571.52 ms | 23% |
| 16-bit | 100 px | 39.94 ms | 27.42 ms | 31% |
| 16-bit | 500 px | 196.86 ms | 134.26 ms | 32% |
| 16-bit | 1000 px | 597.21 ms | 447.68 ms | 25% |

## Tests

- `cargo test -p photocraft-algo --test it -- retouch_sharpen_exact` (2 passed)
- Bit-identical fingerprints between base and this PR at every depth and size.
- Wasm size gate and clean `cargo clippy`.

prs.title: Pencil: keep a 1 px freehand line connected where it turns
prs.body:
Fixes #8040

## Cause
With a 1 px Pencil, `PathWalker::grid_steps` rasterizes each segment of the smoothed stroke on its own line. The last column of a segment can sit up to half a pixel past the segment end, so its minor-axis pixel is extrapolated along that segment. Where a freehand stroke turns, the next segment samples a different line, and its first pixel can land two pixels away from the previous segment's last one. The 1 px line then has a gap (the second screenshot in the issue). Random 6-segment strokes broke this way 189 times out of 2000.

The Shift-click endpoint matrix from the original report already matches the clicked pixels since #8053. I re-checked all TL/TR/BL/BR/C combinations for nine end points at Smoothing 0 and 10 % through the UI path and found no differences.

## Fix
The walker remembers the grid cell of its last step. When a new pixel-grid step does not touch it, `bridge` emits the pixels in between first, so consecutive segments stay 8-connected. Gaps wider than 4 px (a segment cut short by the step budget) are left alone. A straight line split into pieces is already connected, so the #6336 behaviour does not change.

## Verified
- Regression test `pencil_1px_freehand_line_never_breaks_where_it_turns`: fails on `main` without the fix and passes with it (`cargo test -p photocraft-paint --lib pencil_1px_freehand_line_never_breaks_where_it_turns`).
- [x] `cargo xtask ci`: fmt, clippy, layers, scorecard, doctests and wasm pass locally. 27 localization/text UI tests (26 in the `photocraft-ui-egui` lib, plus `camera_raw_localization::all_registered_languages_render_camera_raw_and_switch_without_resetting_view_or_filter`) fail on this macOS machine because it has no CJK system fonts (`No glyph for "模"`). The same tests fail on `main` without this change.

🤖 Generated with AI, see the Co-Authored-By trailers for the models

approval.body:
Reviewed at 652075f (`dynamics.rs` and the new test in `brush_tests.rs`, the whole diff).

Cause and fix, as the code shows them: on the pixel-grid path each segment of a freehand stroke is rasterized on its own line, so where the stroke turns the next segment's first pixel can sit two cells from the previous one's last and the 1 px line has a gap. `PathWalker` now remembers the grid cell of the last emitted step (`cell`, set in `emit`, so the filler pixels also update it) and `bridge` fills the cells between it and the next step before that step is emitted.

Checked: `bridge` only runs on grid steps, and only when the gap is at most `MAX_BRIDGE` (4 px) on the larger axis, so a step cut off by the walker's budget is not smeared; it stops once the next cell is within 1.5 on both axes, moving at most one cell per axis per fill, so it terminates in at most four iterations and a diagonal or straight gap is filled with one connected path; `cell` starts as `None` in the constructor, so the first step of a stroke has nothing to bridge to. The new test draws 300 random 7-point strokes with a 1 px aliased tip and asserts the painted pixels are one 8-connected component; it reproduces the report (#8040) and would fail on the gap. The hosted gate is green at this head.

Not verified: I did not run the test, and I did not check whether the bridge can add a pixel the old path did not paint at the very first cell after `pixel_grid` is re-armed in a long-running walker (the walker is built per stroke in the paths I read).

APPROVE.

prs.title: fix(ui): the Color panel remembers its options across restarts
prs.body:
Fixes #9592.

The Color panel forgot its options on every restart: what it shows (Hue Cube, RGB/HSB/… Sliders, Color Wheel), its ramp, Make Ramp Web Safe and which chip it edits. Its state (`ColorPanelState`) is serializable, but nothing saved it. The dock layout goes to the preferences (`panelLayout`), and `ui.ron` holds only eframe's window and egui state.

### Photoshop's behaviour

Photoshop keeps the Color panel's options (its panel menu choices) across restarts. I couldn't recheck it tonight, because Photoshop stopped answering scripts in my session.

### What changes

- **`Preferences::color_panel`:** a new field holding the options as JSON owned by the shell, like `panel_layout`. `serde(default)` reads older preference files fine.
- **`color_panel_ui::persist`:** writes them when they change, a small JSON compare per frame next to `dock::persist`.
- **`color_panel_ui::restore`:** reads them at launch next to `dock::restore`. Missing or unreadable options keep the defaults.
- This is separate from workspaces: switching a workspace doesn't change the panel's options.

### Verification

Live app with a scratch settings folder: `ui.set {"colorPanel": {"mode": "hsbSliders", "ramp": "grayscaleRamp"}}`, quit, relaunch:

| | main | this PR | Photoshop |
|---|---|---|---|
| Color panel after a restart | Hue Cube, RGB Spectrum (defaults); nothing in `preferences.json` or `ui.ron` | HSB Sliders, Grayscale Ramp | options kept |

### Tests

- `color_panel_tests::color_panel_options_survive_a_restart`: a mode and ramp go through the preferences into a new app; empty preferences keep the defaults. Without saving it comes back as (HueCube, RgbSpectrum).
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for engine and ui-egui; `cargo test -p photocraft-engine -p photocraft-ui-egui` (with `CRAFT_FONTS_DIR`); `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`.

prs.title: fix(ui): the layer list doesn't move with no layer selected
prs.body:
Fixes #9546.

With no layer selected, the Layers panel shows the Blend/Opacity and Lock/Fill rows greyed out (#8880), and the layer list starts lower than with a layer selected. In the Studio and Classic themes the first layer row moves down 6 points. Cause: the greyed-out rows were drawn inside one `add_enabled_ui(false, …)` wrapper. A child UI adds one more item gap after itself, which the active layer's rows (two `ui.horizontal`s) don't have. The Pro themes' docks have zero item spacing, so they didn't show it.

### Photoshop's behaviour

Photoshop keeps the layer list in place whether or not a layer is selected; only the rows above grey out. I didn't open Photoshop for this: Photoshop stopped answering scripts in my session tonight, and the expected layout is the panel's own selected state.

### What changes

`panels.rs` `inactive_blend_rows` has no disabled wrapper any more. Each of its two rows is a `ui.horizontal` that disables itself (`ui.disable()`), so its layout is the same as the active layer's rows.

### Verification

|---|---|---|
| Studio, selected / none | 578 / 584 | 578 / 578 |
| Classic, selected / none | 578 / 584 | 578 / 578 |
| Pro Medium, selected / none | 594 / 594 | 594 / 594 |

### Tests

- `layer_pct_slider_tests::layer_rows_do_not_move_when_no_layer_is_selected`: the first row's top is the same with and without a selected layer, in Studio, Classic and Pro Medium. On main it fails in Studio (584 vs 578).

prs.title: fix(io): drop a kept Txt2 once no type layers are left
prs.body:
Fixes the first problem in #9563 (the orphaned `Txt2`; the issue lists others).

A PSD saved from Photoshop with type layers carries a document-level `Txt2` block: the text engine's fonts and layout caches. Once every type layer was deleted, PhotoCraft still wrote that block back unchanged on save. It describes text that no longer exists, and the report measured it at 86 % of one saved file. With type layers present, the export already regenerates `Txt2`. Only the "no type layers left" case fell through to the preserved copy.

### Photoshop's behaviour

Per the report: open a PSD with type layers, delete all of them, and save. Photoshop's file has no `Txt2` block. I couldn't rerun this in Photoshop myself tonight, because Photoshop stopped answering scripts in my session. The behaviour is simple to state and matches what the exporter already does when type layers are present.

### What changes

`psd_export`: the preserved `Txt2` is skipped when the document has no type layers, as well as when a fresh one is generated. All other preserved global blocks are untouched.

### Verification

| PSD with a kept `Txt2`, no type layers left | main | this PR | Photoshop (reporter) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Txt2` in the saved file | kept, byte for byte | absent | absent |
| with a type layer (control) | regenerated | regenerated | present |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

prs.title: fix(compose, gpu): a Pass Through group with Blend If renders isolated
prs.body:
Fixes #9554.

A Pass Through group composites its children straight into the backdrop, so an adjustment inside it changes the layers beneath. Photoshop renders such a group isolated, like Normal, in a few cases: below 100 % Fill, and as a clip base that holds an adjustment. PhotoCraft already handles those. Per the report, a group that has its own Blend If is another such case: Photoshop keeps the stored mode Pass Through, but its pixels match an isolated group. PhotoCraft kept compositing straight through, so the group's Invert child inverted the layer beneath before Blend If was even applied.

### Photoshop's behaviour

From the report's Photoshop 27.11 runs: (64, 128, 192), then above it a Pass Through group holding only an Invert, with the group's Red › Underlying Layer white point at 110.
- Photoshop leaves the backdrop at (64, 128, 192).
- Removing the group's Blend If, or moving the same range onto the child, inverts it.
- A Normal group with the same range leaves it alone.

I couldn't rerun this myself: Photoshop stopped answering scripts in my session tonight. The reporter's controls separate the cases cleanly, and they match the existing isolation rule.

### What changes

The pass-through shortcut in `compose::composite_layer`, and its mirror in the GPU planner's `layer_plain`, are skipped when the group has active Blend If (`blend_if_active`). The group then takes the isolated path both compositors already use below 100 % Fill.

### Verification

| (64, 128, 192) under a Pass Through group with an Invert | main | this PR | Photoshop 27.11 (reporter) |
|---|---|---|---|
| group Red › Underlying white 110 | (191, 127, 63) | (64, 128, 192) | (64, 128, 192) |
| no group Blend If (control) | (191, 127, 63) | (191, 127, 63) | inverted |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- `change_bounds` and the pass-through adjustment checks (around lines 1661 and 1692) still treat such a group as reaching the layers beneath. That over-estimates the redraw area, which is safe.

### Tests

- `compose::tests::pass_through_group_with_blend_if_is_isolated`: both rows of the table. On main it fails with (191, 127, 63), the reporter's PhotoCraft output.
- `gpu` `parity::pass_through_group_with_blend_if_is_isolated`: the same group, with and without Blend If, over a noise backdrop. Without the planner change it is 255 levels off.
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for compose and gpu; `cargo test -p photocraft-compose -p photocraft-gpu`; `cargo xtask test-corpus`; `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`.

prs.title: fix(engine): copied type keeps its size across resolutions after an edit
prs.body:
Fixes #9560.

A type layer copied to a document of another resolution (Duplicate Layer to another document, dragging a layer across, or pasting a copied layer) looked right at first. On its next text edit it re-laid out at the destination's resolution: a 24 pt line from a 72 ppi document grew about 4.2× in a 300 ppi one, and shrank the other way. Text is laid out at `pt × dpi / 72`, and the copies kept the source's point size and box at the destination's dpi.

### Photoshop's behaviour

Per the report (Photoshop 27.11), Photoshop keeps the pixels and adapts the point size: 24 pt from 72 ppi becomes 5.76 pt at 300 ppi, and from 300 to 72 ppi becomes 100 pt. Later edits keep that size. I couldn't rerun this in Photoshop myself tonight, because Photoshop stopped answering scripts in my session.

### What changes

`layer_copy_cmds::adapt_copies`, the step both routes use to fit copied layers to the destination, now runs `canvas_geom::set_resolution` on the copies for the destination's resolution. That is the same compensation Image › Image Size already applies when only the resolution changes:
- box and path text scale with the dpi ratio;
- the layer transform undoes it;
- the PSD `TySh` is retagged.

The pixels are what Photoshop's adapted point size gives. The type model keeps its point size with a compensating transform, as after Image Size. A rendered copy is unchanged; only later edits now keep the size.

### Verification

| 24 pt "H", copied, then edited M → H | main | this PR | Photoshop 27.11 (reporter) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 72 → 300 ppi, ink after the edit | about 4.2× larger (58 × 73 vs 14 × 18 here) | same as the source | same as the source |
| 300 → 72 ppi | about 4.2× smaller | same as the source | same as the source |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- The Character panel shows the original point size (24 pt) on the copy, with the scale in its transform, as after an Image Size resolution change. Photoshop shows the adapted size (5.76 pt). Rewriting the point size instead would be a separate change touching every type run, so I kept to the existing mechanism.

### Tests

- `layer_copy_cmds::tests::copied_type_keeps_its_pixel_size_across_resolutions_after_an_edit`: 72→300 and 300→72 ppi, copy, then edit "H" → "M" → "H"; the bounds match the source's. Without the change it fails 72→300 with a 58 × 73 box against 14 × 18.
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for engine; `cargo test -p photocraft-engine`; `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

prs.title: fix(io): PSD layer-effect contours keep at most 16 points
prs.body:
Fixes #9556.

PhotoCraft wrote every point of a layer-effect contour into the PSD's effects descriptor (`ShpC` › `Crv `). Photoshop reads at most 16. A longer contour makes it report "A problem was encountered reading layer … because of a program error" and load the layer without any effects. The issue lists six built-in contours longer than 16 points: Cone, Cone - Inverted, Ring, Ring - Double, Rolling Slope - Descending and Rounded Steps. Any effect using one of them (Bevel & Emboss gloss and contour, Satin, shadows, glows) lost the whole style in Photoshop.

### Photoshop's behaviour

- The reporter checked the limit in Photoshop 2026: 16 points load, while 17 and 27 fail and drop the effects.

prs.title: fix(compose, gpu): an adjustment layer's This Layer range judges its result before Opacity
prs.body:
Fixes #9542.

An adjustment layer has no pixels of its own, so its Blend If "This Layer" ranges have to judge something else. PhotoCraft used the composite after Opacity and the mask had already mixed the result into the backdrop. Photoshop judges the adjustment's result at full strength. So below 100 % Opacity, or under a partial mask, a range could hide an effect Photoshop keeps, or let through one it drops.

### Photoshop's behaviour

Photoshop 2025 (26.2), by script on a synthetic 2×2 RGB 8-bit document filled with (64, 128, 192), with an Invert adjustment layer at 40 % Opacity on top. Read back from a flattened copy:

| Blend If on the Invert layer | Photoshop |
|---|---|
| Red › This Layer, black point 150 | (115, 128, 140): kept, since Invert's red 191 passes 150 |
| Red › This Layer, white point 150 | (64, 128, 192): dropped |
| none (control) | (115, 128, 140) |

These match the reporter's Photoshop 27.11 numbers.

### What changes

- **`compose::apply_blend_if`:** for an adjustment layer, This Layer is the adjustment applied to the backdrop (the `before` buffer), before Opacity and the mask mix it in. It is also taken before the layer's blend mode; I measured Normal only, so that part is an assumption.
- **`gpu` planner `blend_if`:** passes the same unmixed result as C, from an extra `adjust` pass on the retained backdrop, instead of judging B (the mixed composite).
  - The shader already reads C when `p4.y` is clear; only its comment changes.

Underlying Layer, pixel layers and groups are unchanged.

### Verification

| Invert at 40 % over (64, 128, 192) | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Red This Layer black 150 | (64, 128, 192): dropped | (115, 128, 140) | (115, 128, 140) |
| Red This Layer white 150 | (115, 128, 140): leaked | (64, 128, 192) | (64, 128, 192) |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- Clipped layers above an adjustment no longer count towards its This Layer value: the judgement is the adjustment's own result. The reporter's follow-up says partial masks behave like Opacity here, and both are now outside the judgement.
- The GPU adds one adjustment pass for an adjustment layer that has Blend If. Others are unaffected.

### Tests

- `compose::tests::adjustment_blend_if_judges_the_result_before_opacity`: both rows above. On main it fails with (64, 128, 192) for the black point, the reporter's output.
- `gpu` `parity::blend_if`: its adjustment case now runs at 40 % Opacity. Without the planner change it fails by 94 levels (U8 gray this hard).
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for compose and gpu; `cargo test -p photocraft-compose -p photocraft-gpu`; `cargo xtask test-corpus`; `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`.

prs.title: fix(compose, gpu): Blend If hard points match Photoshop at 16 bits and for Gray
prs.body:
Fixes #9521. Fixes #9522.

Two Blend If precision fixes in the same few lines, from the same report bundle.

## #9521: 16-bit values at a hard point

A 16-bit pixel right at a hard Blend If point fell on the wrong side of it. `blend_if_level` read a channel as `x · 255` and snapped only within 1e-4 of a whole level. So RGB16 32895 read as level 127.996, below a hard black point at 128, and the layer was hidden where Photoshop shows it. The same happens at white points, one step past the level.

### Photoshop's behaviour

Photoshop 2025 (26.2), by script on synthetic 2×2 16-bit RGB documents: a white layer over a grey background, with Blend If › Blue › Underlying Layer set to a hard black point (then a hard white point) at levels 1, 64, 128 and 200. I swept the background over Photoshop's 16-bit steps n (its 0–32768 scale, written as 2n in a 16-bit raw export) and read a flattened copy:

| Cutoff level c | `c · 32768 / 255` | black point: first step shown | white point: last step shown |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 128.50 | 129 | 129 |
| 64 | 8224.13 | 8224 | 8224 |
| 128 | 16448.25 | 16448 | 16448 |
| 200 | 25700.39 | 25700 | 25700 |

So Photoshop compares at its 16-bit precision. A hard point at level `c` sits on step `round(c · 32768 / 255)`, and a value on that step passes both a black point and a white point there. RGB16 32895 is step 16448, level 128's step, which is why Photoshop keeps the layer the reporter describes.

### What changes

- **`compose::blend_if_level`:** a value whose step `round(x · 32768)` equals its nearest level's step `round(c · 32768 / 255)` is exactly that level; anything else stays `x · 255`.
  - Every 8-bit level is on its own step, so 8-bit behaviour is unchanged. That includes the "a few millionths off" drift the old 1e-4 snap was there for (`blend_if_hard_point_includes_its_own_level` still passes).
- **`compose.wgsl` `blend_if_weight`:** the GPU snaps the same way.
  - 16- and 32-bit layers reach the GPU as half-float, so GPU hard points at those depths stay approximate, as the `blend_if` parity test already notes.

### Verification (#9521)

| RGB16 backdrop under a white layer, Underlying Blue black point 128 | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32895 (step 16448) | hidden: backdrop (32895…) | white | white |
| 32894 (step 16447) | hidden | hidden | hidden |

The new test also checks every black and white cutoff in the table above, at the step and one past it.


## #9522: Gray on mixed 8-bit colours

Blend If's Gray used Rec. 601 luma, 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B, unrounded. Photoshop's Gray differs in both weights and rounding. With the same scripted setup on an 8-bit document (a white layer over one backdrop colour, a hard Gray point on Underlying Layer), I binary-searched the first shown value of pure red, green and blue against black points at 20, 25 and 28:

| Channel | black 20 | black 25 | black 28 |
|---|---|---|---|
| R | 65 hidden / 66 shown | 81 / 82 | 91 / 92 |
| G | 33 / 34 | 41 / 42 | 46 / 47 |
| B | 177 / 178 | 222 / 223 | 250 / 251 |

Every boundary fits Gray = (30 R + 59 G + 11 B) / 100, rounded half down. For example, R 65 → 19.5 → 19 is hidden and B 250 → 27.5 → 27 is hidden, while R 66 → 19.8 → 20 and B 251 → 27.61 → 28 are shown. So do the reporter's colours, which Photoshop keeps and PhotoCraft hid:

| Backdrop colour, Gray point | Rec. 601 (main) | Photoshop's Gray | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (123, 126, 151), black 128 | 127.95 → hidden | 127.85 → 128 | hidden | shown | shown |
| (120, 129, 149), white 128 | 128.59 → hidden | 128.5 → 128 | hidden | shown | shown |
| (121, 129, 149), white 128 (control) | 128.89 → hidden | 128.8 → 129 | hidden | hidden | hidden |

**Change:** `compose::blend_if_gray`, with the same arithmetic in `compose.wgsl` `blend_if_weight`. On whole levels Gray is `⌊(30 R + 59 G + 11 B + 49) / 100⌋`; between levels (deeper documents) it is the unrounded `(30 R + 59 G + 11 B) / 100`.

## Both

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- 32-bit documents use the same rule, so a float within half a 16-bit step of a level now counts as that level. Before, it was within 1e-4. I haven't measured Photoshop's 32-bit Blend If.
- Gray on 16- and 32-bit documents: only the weights are measured (on 8-bit). Values between levels keep the unrounded weighting, which is an assumption.

### Tests

- `compose::tests::blend_if_gray_follows_photoshops_weights_and_rounding`: the seven measured single-channel boundaries and the reporter's colours. With Rec. 601 it fails at the first case (red 66 under black 20).
- `compose::tests::blend_if_16_bit_cutoffs_follow_photoshops_steps`: the four measured cutoffs, black and white, at the step and the next, plus the reporter's 32895/32894 boundary. On main it fails ("white 1: step 129 shows").
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for compose and gpu; `cargo test -p photocraft-compose -p photocraft-gpu` (including the `blend_if` parity test); `cargo xtask test-corpus`; `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`.

prs.title: Fix Type on a Path wrapping and caret positioning across closed-path seams
prs.body:
Closed-path text clips at the path's first knot even when unused circumference remains. Caret projection also needs to use the same wrapped text interval. Starting near the upper-left seam of an ellipse or the left side of a rectangle exposes this behaviour.

Wrap closed-path arc-length sampling and inverse caret projection across the seam. Limit glyph centres to one circuit, using aligned layout bounds to support centred and right-aligned text. Preserve open-path endpoint behaviour and current area-type routing.

Synthetic regression coverage includes rectangle seams, reversed/flipped ellipse geometry, one-circuit clipping, alignment, open endpoints and inverse projection. A UI test checks actual caret indices 1, 4, 7 and 10 using an independent document-space rectangle oracle, including seam crossing.

Validation against upstream b07b7fab559ce2f7c3ba7ef80b7fb50c3aad170e:

- Baseline: three intended text assertion failures, one passing open-path control; corrected caret assertion returns 0 instead of 1. Both Cargo test commands exit 101 after compiling and executing tests.
- Fixed: text library 232 passed/5 ignored; UI type suite 145 passed/2 ignored; zero failures. Focused corrected caret test passes separately and is included in the UI suite total.
- Formatting, whitespace, Clippy with -D warnings, dependency layering (31 crates) and native application cargo check pass.

WASM, real-file corpora and isolated GUI verification remain unperformed. Current upstream main and comprehensive competing-PR clearance require refresh before submission. The existing block v0.1.6 future-compatibility warning is nonfatal. This corrects existing Type on a Path functionality; preserve its original contributor attribution (PR #5180).

This is an independent correction to Type on a Path from #5180. It overlaps #5230; this submission will disclose its live disposition and does not ask maintainers to wait for it. No Work Path preview, component selection, component transforms or Shape dragging is included.

prs.title: fix(compose, gpu): adjustment layers apply Fill inside the special eight blend modes
prs.body:
Fixes #9501.

An adjustment layer below 100 % Fill in one of Photoshop's "special eight" blend modes faded its blend by Fill, as if Fill were Opacity. The eight are Color Burn, Linear Burn, Color Dodge, Linear Dodge, Vivid Light, Linear Light, Hard Mix and Difference. In those modes Photoshop applies Fill *inside* the blend: the result is pulled toward the mode's neutral colour, then blended at Opacity. PhotoCraft already does this for pixel layers (`psblend::composite_fill`). The adjustment branch multiplied Fill into the coverage on both the CPU (`compose::blend_back`) and the GPU (`AdjMix`).

### Photoshop's behaviour

Photoshop 2025 (26.2), by script on a synthetic 4×4 RGB 8-bit document filled with (64, 128, 192). On top, a Levels adjustment layer with Output 128–128, i.e. a constant 0.5. Read back from a flattened copy:

| Levels layer | Photoshop |
|---|---|
| Color Dodge, Fill 40 % | (80, 160, 240) |
| Linear Burn, Fill 40 % | (13, 77, 141) |
| Normal, Fill 40 % (control) | (90, 128, 166) |
| Color Dodge, Fill 100 % (control) | (129, 255, 255) |

These match the reporter's Photoshop 27.11 numbers for a constant-0.5 Color Lookup. They also match the pixel-layer rule: 64 / (1 − 0.4·0.5) = 80, and 64 + (1 − 0.6·0.5) − 1 → 13.

### What changes

- **`compose` (CPU):**
  - With Fill < 100 % in a special-eight mode, the adjustment branch blends with `psblend::blend_rgb_fill(mode, backdrop, result, fill)`, at coverage Opacity × mask.
  - Every other mode, or Fill 100 %, is unchanged (Fill × Opacity as coverage).
- **`gpu`:**
  - The planner passes Opacity and Fill separately to `AdjMix` (`adjustment_fill`).
  - `fs_adjmix` pulls the result toward the neutral colour, as `composite_fill` does. It keeps a single `blend_rgb` call, per the shader's note on WARP compile time.

### Verification

`photocraft-cli run` on a new 4×4 document: fill `#4080c0`, a Levels layer with output 128–128, then `layer.setProps {blend, fill: 0.4}`, then `document.pixel`:

| | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Color Dodge, Fill 40 % | (90, 179, 217) | (80, 160, 240) | (80, 160, 240) |
| Linear Burn, Fill 40 % | (38, 77, 141) | (13, 77, 141) | (13, 77, 141) |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- This touches `blend_back`, which my #9509 (#9483, the f32 cancellation over huge HDR values) also changes, on the line next to this one. Whichever merges second needs a one-line rebase, and I'll do it.
- Dissolve, the adjustment layer's own clipped layers and the Fill = 0 early-out keep their current paths.

### Tests

- `compose::tests::adjustment_fill_changes_the_special_blend_modes`: Color Dodge and Linear Burn at 40 % Fill give Photoshop's values within one level. Without the change it gives (90, 179, 217), the reporter's PhotoCraft output.
- `gpu` `parity::special_eight_fill_on_adjustment_layers_matches_cpu`: all eight modes at Fill 30 % and 60 %, Opacity 70 %, over an opaque noise backdrop. Without the GPU change it fails by 53 levels (Color Burn).
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for compose and gpu; `cargo test -p photocraft-compose -p photocraft-gpu`; `cargo xtask test-corpus`; `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`.

prs.title: fix: an edit at full coverage keeps its result over huge 32-bit values
prs.body:
Fixes #9483.

In a 32-bit document, a Color Lookup (or any edit) at full strength over very large pixel values could lose its result. A constant-0.1 look over 2²⁰ gave 0.125, and a 0.5 look over 1e8 gave 0. Every blend back to the original pixel computed `o + (r − o)·k`. In f32, `r − o` has already rounded away a result that small against `o`, and adding `o` back can't recover it.

### Photoshop's behaviour

I didn't reproduce this in Photoshop: loading a .cube into a 32-bit Color Lookup by script needs descriptor keys I couldn't confirm. The reporter ran Photoshop 27.11 on this case: at 100 % the bounded LUT output is kept for inputs of 1, 1,000,000 and 100,000,000 (≈ (0.1, 0.9, 0.4) for their cube; 0.5000076 for a constant look). The expectation is that full coverage gives the edit's result, whatever the backdrop.

### What changes

The three blends that mix an edit back over the original now compute `o·(1−k) + r·k`:
- `photocraft-compose` `blend_back`: adjustment layers.
- `photocraft-engine` `pixels::mix_through_selection`: destructive edits, with or without a selection.
- `photocraft-plugins` `apply`: plug-in filters through a selection, which must stay bit-identical to the built-in route (`example_invert_matches_builtin_invert…` checks that).

At k = 1 this is exactly `r`. At k = 0 it is exactly `o`, and k = 0 pixels are skipped anyway. In between, it differs from the old form only in the last bit.

### Verification

`photocraft-cli run` on a new 4×4 32-bit document: fill white, then Exposure +20 (pixels 1,048,576), then Color Lookup with an invented constant-0.1 cube, then `document.pixel`:

| | main | this PR | Photoshop 27.11 (reporter) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Image › Adjustments › Color Lookup | 0.125 | 0.1 | LUT output kept |
| Color Lookup adjustment layer | 0.125 | 0.1 | LUT output kept |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- Two bit-exact oracles change with the formula: `reused_render_matches_previous_allocating_stack`'s reference stack, and `mix_through_selection`'s selection test. Both now spell the new formula; their tolerances are unchanged.

prs.title: fix(ui): Keyboard Shortcuts records ⌘Z instead of undoing the capture
prs.body:
Fixes #9487.

In Edit › Keyboard Shortcuts, pressing ⌘Z (Ctrl+Z on Windows and Linux) in a shortcut field never recorded it. The field went back to its old shortcut and stopped waiting for keys. Every other key worked.

Cause: the dialog keeps its own ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z history (#4697, `edit_history::keys`). Clicking the field to start the capture is one step of that history, so ⌘Z undid that click before the field could read the key.

### Photoshop's behaviour

Photoshop 2025 (26.2) on macOS, with a new 200×100 document: Edit › Keyboard Shortcuts, click the empty shortcut of File › Open as Smart Object…, press ⌘Z. The field shows **⌘+Z** with a warning: "⌘+Z is already in use and will be removed from Edit > Undo if accepted." I cancelled the dialog afterwards, so nothing was saved.

### What changes

`crates/ui-egui/src/edit_history.rs`:
- While the front dialog has a field waiting for keys (`capture: true`), ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z are left to that field, which records them like any other key.
- Outside a capture, ⌘Z still steps the dialog back. A step no longer restores the "waiting for keys" state of the click that started a capture, so the next key isn't silently captured.

### Verification

Live app (control channel, scratch settings folder): Edit › Keyboard Shortcuts, click File › Open…'s shortcut, press ⌘Z.

| | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⌘Z in a waiting shortcut field | capture ends, Open keeps its old key | Open gets ⌘Z, with "⌘Z is already in use by Edit › Undo and will be removed from it when you click OK." | ⌘+Z recorded, "already in use and will be removed from Edit > Undo if accepted" |
| ⌘Z again (not capturing) | – | the change is undone, the field isn't waiting for keys | – (Photoshop's dialog has an Undo button) |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- The guard reads the dialog field `capture`, which only the shortcut dialogs set. Other parameter dialogs keep their ⌘Z history unchanged.
- Rebinding Undo itself (the reporter sets ⌘Z to Toggle Last State and ⇧⌘Z to Undo) works through the same capture. The usual conflict message tells the user that Undo loses ⌘Z.

### Tests

- `prefs_ui::shortcut_capture_tests::cmd_z_is_recorded_while_capturing_and_undoes_otherwise`:
  - ⌘Z captured on Edit › Search is stored as `Cmd+Z`;
  - a following ⌘Z undoes it and leaves capture off.
  - It fails without the guard (nothing recorded) and without the capture reset ("doesn't wait for keys again").
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for ui-egui; `cargo test -p photocraft-ui-egui` (3826 + 133); `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`. All pass.

prs.title: fix(vector): a mask feather continues the mask past the canvas edge
prs.body:
Fixes #9475.

A feathered layer mask came out too bright where the canvas cut the feather off. The result also changed when the canvas was taller with the same mask. The blur (`photocraft_vector::feather::gaussian`, shared by pixel masks, vector masks and soft shape layers) clamped **each** of its three box passes at the plane's edge. The plane stops at the canvas, so passes 2 and 3 repeated already-blurred values past it.

### Photoshop's behaviour

Photoshop 2025 (26.2) on macOS, driven by script on synthetic 256×128 RGB 8-bit documents: black background, a white layer, a mask from a rectangular selection with no anti-aliasing (Reveal Selection), then the mask's Feather set in Properties.
- Mask rectangle x 64–191, y 32–95, Feather 32 px: the canvas edges stay dark, as if the black mask continued past the canvas.
- Mask white over the left half and the full height, Feather 32 px: every row is identical, so the top and bottom edges don't darken. The mask continues past the edge with its edge values (white there).

The new blur pads the plane with its edge values by the passes' reach (`3 × (r + 1)`), blurs, and keeps the original area. Both cases come out as Photoshop's.

### Verification

Same steps with `photocraft-cli run` (main = upstream 528491f9a), compared pixel by pixel with Photoshop's output:

| Feather 32 px | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| interior rectangle, max difference from Photoshop | 12 levels (bottom edge, 53 vs 41) | 1 level | – |
| same mask on a 256×384 canvas, centre crop vs the 256×128 result | 12 levels apart | identical | identical (#9475) |
| mask white up to the edge, max difference from Photoshop | 1 | 1 | rows identical |

With the plane's edge inside constant mask, padding changes nothing: interior feathers of 1–4 px are byte-identical to main.

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- **#9476 is not fixed here.** Small feathers (1 px is 8 levels off at the rectangle's corner, 2 px is 4 levels off) are a separate kernel-shape difference. From 4 px up, main's three box passes already match Photoshop within a level. I measured 0.5–8 px in Photoshop, and below about 3 px neither box passes nor a Gaussian of variance f² fits within a level. So I left that one alone rather than tune a constant.
- Memory: the edge continuation is done line by line (each row, then each column, padded by `3 × (r + 1)` on its own), so it needs only per-line buffers, not a padded copy of the plane. If a line's buffers can't be reserved, those lines are left unblurred rather than aborting. `padding_each_line_matches_padding_the_plane` checks that this is bitwise identical to padding the whole plane.
- `parallel_gaussian_matches_the_sequential_reference` now checks the parallel and sequential blurs agree both without and with the edge padding.

### Tests

- `masks::tests::feather_at_the_canvas_edge_continues_the_mask_past_it`:
  - a 32 px feathered rectangle gives the same values on a taller canvas;
  - a mask white up to the edge keeps every row equal and the edge white.
  - It fails without the padding (0.093 apart, about 24 levels).
- `soft_shape_matches_an_equal_vector_mask` gains a 40 px case that reaches the canvas edge.
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for vector and compose; `cargo test -p photocraft-vector -p photocraft-compose`; `cargo xtask test-corpus`; `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`. All pass.

- The mask blur now continues each line past its ends with its edge values, so a feather that reaches the canvas edge sees the mask carrying on, as the author reports Photoshop does (#9475), rather than clamping every box pass at the edge, which brightened the feather there.

A test checks the largest buffer stays within the plane size at the maximum feather, and the parallel and sequential paths are compared for both halo 0 and the real halo.

prs.title: fix(ui): new layer effects start from the Make Default values
prs.body:
Fixes #9477.

Make Default in the Layer Style dialog stored the page's values (`layer.layerStyle.makeDefault`), and Reset to Default read them back. But a **new** effect always started from the factory defaults, so the saved default never appeared. For example: set a Stroke's Size, click Make Default, Cancel, and open Layer Style › Stroke… again. The stroke is back to 1 px Inside.

### Photoshop's behaviour

After Make Default, new effects of that kind start from the saved values. Reset to Default brings those values back too. I didn't click Make Default in the installed Photoshop 2025, because it changes that copy's stored preferences. The behaviour above comes from public sources: a [Photoshop Training Channel tip on the Make Default button](https://photoshoptrainingchannel.com/tips/make-default-button-layer-style-panel/) and an [Adobe community thread on resetting layer style defaults](https://community.adobe.com/t5/photoshop-ecosystem-discussions/how-to-reset-the-default-values-of-layer-styles/m-p/14477436).

### What changes

All in `crates/ui-egui/src/layer_style.rs`:
- `open` seeds the dialog's fields with the session's user defaults (`initial_fields_with`, `userDefaults`). `initial_fields` keeps its signature and passes an empty map.
- `add_instance` and `fresh_params` lay a kind's user default over its factory defaults. Keys the default doesn't hold keep their factory values. All three ways of adding an effect go through `add_instance`: opening the dialog on an effect the layer doesn't have, the list's checkbox, and the "+" button.
- Make Default also updates the dialog's copy, so a "+" in the same dialog starts from it.

### Verification

Live app with a scratch settings folder, on a new 300×200 document with an empty layer: Layer › Layer Style › Stroke…, Size 7, Make Default, Cancel, then Layer › Layer Style › Stroke… again.

| | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stroke page after reopening | Size 1 (factory) | Size 7 (the made default) | the made default (public docs, see above) |
| New Drop Shadow (no default made) | factory | factory | factory |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- The fix is in the dialog only. Engine commands that add effects with explicit params (`layer.layerStyle.stroke`, scripts, presets) are unchanged, so scripted results don't depend on a user's saved defaults.
- Effects already on a layer keep their own values, as in Photoshop. Only new instances use the default.

### Tests

- `layer_style::tests::new_effects_start_from_the_made_default`:
  - saves a Stroke default (Size 7, Outside);
  - opens the dialog on Stroke and adds a second stroke with "+"; both start at 7 / Outside, and Opacity keeps the factory value;
  - a new Drop Shadow keeps the factory size.
  - It fails without the overlay (left `(1, "inside")`, right `(7, "outside")`).

prs.title: fix(text): vertical type sets roman letters upright, one per em, as Photoshop does (#9470)
prs.body:
Fixes #9470.

Vertical type laid Latin letters and digits on their side: the word was turned 90° and ran down the column, so "VERTICAL" read sideways. `layout.rs` documented that as "Photoshop's default". Photoshop's Vertical Type tool stacks roman letters **upright, one character per em** down the column.

### Photoshop's behaviour

Photoshop 2025 (26.2) on macOS, on synthetic documents:
- **Vertical Type tool** (full-screen control): click, type "ABC", commit. The letters stand upright, stacked. The layer's `textStyle.baselineDirection` reads **withStream**, and the saved PSD's style run has `/BaselineDirection 1`.
- **Script**: a vertical "VERTICAL" layer in Arial at 36 px measures **26 × 278 px**, which is 7 em steps of 36 px plus a capital's height. Setting `baselineDirection` to **rotated** lays the word on its side, **28 × 174 px**, and the PSD then stores `/BaselineDirection 2`.
- The document's default style sheet says `/BaselineDirection 2`. The tool overrides it with 1 in each run, so a run without its own value falls back to rotated.

### What changes

- **doc**: `CharStyle::rotate_roman` (false = upright, the default; `serde(default)`).
- **text/psd**: `BaselineDirection` is read into `rotate_roman` (2 = rotated) through the usual style-sheet lookup, so a run without its own value gets the sheet's. It's written back as 1 or 2.
- **text/layout**: in vertical type, roman characters (UAX #50 "rotated" class, whitespace aside) go through the existing upright path unless their run sets `rotate_roman`:
  - Each takes **one em** down the column. A second shaping pass gives each character the letter spacing that turns its shaped advance into the em, the same way tabs are already widened.
  - Pair kerning (`kern`) is off between the stacked letters.
  - CJK text is unchanged: it stands upright either way.
- `type_styles_cmds`' perturbed style covers the new field.

### Verification

`photocraft-cli run --new 400×500 --cmd type.create {"text":"VERTICAL","orientation":"vertical","font":"Arial","size":36}`, flattened, ink bounding box:

| | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| default vertical type | 27 × 173 (sideways) | 25 × 277 (upright stack) | 26 × 278 (Vertical Type tool default) |
| `BaselineDirection 2` / rotated | – | sideways, as before | 28 × 174 |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- **Existing documents:** vertical text in `.pcraft` files saved before this change has no `rotate_roman`, so it now renders upright, like new vertical type in Photoshop. PSDs keep whatever their runs (or style sheet) say.
- **Not in this PR:** a Character panel menu toggle (Photoshop's "Standard Vertical Roman Alignment") to switch a selection between upright and rotated. The style field and PSD round trip are there for it.
- `cargo test --workspace` (plugins excluded) passes, except `photocraft`'s `single_instance::tests::a_sandboxed_second_launch_hands_its_paths_over_a_unix_socket`. It passed one of three reruns and this PR doesn't touch it.

### Tests

- `vertical_tests::latin_stands_upright_one_per_em_by_default`: "VERTICAL" at 36 px is all upright glyphs, 36 px apart in one column; rendered it's a narrow stack about 8 em tall, taller than the rotated word. It fails without the layout change.
- `psd::…::baseline_direction_round_trips`: run value 1 beats a sheet's 2; a run without one takes the sheet's; none at all is upright; both values write back. It fails without the PSD read.
- The rotated-Latin tests now ask for `rotate_roman` explicitly. The CJK test expects Latin inside vertical CJK upright by default and rotated when asked.
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for doc and text; `cargo test --workspace --exclude photocraft-plugins --no-fail-fast` (only the flaky test above failing); `cargo xtask test-corpus` (4764 passed); `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`. All pass.

prs.title: fix(io): import a Displace smart filter that names its map file without embedding it (#9162)
prs.body:
Fixes #9162.

## Root cause

#3673 (PR #3680) imports a Displace smart filter only when its map is embedded in `DspD`. Photoshop can also save a Displace that only names the map file in `DspF` (a `Pth ` value) with no `DspD` (ag-psd models the filter with `DspF` only). For that shape `import_params` returned `None`, so the filter became `psd.unsupportedFilter` ("Displace...") and `layer.smartObjects.replaceContents` reported "not supported" and passed the pixels through, the exact warning in the issue. Re-render could already read a `mapPath` through the document path policy (`filters_ext::resolve_map_path`, #3670); import just never produced one.

## Change (`crates/io/src/displace_map.rs`)

- `fltr_path` decodes a `Pth ` `DspF` (`txtu`, u32 LE size, u32 LE UTF-16 unit count, UTF-16LE path, NUL). All lengths are checked; malformed data returns `None`, never panics.
- `import_params` falls back to that path as `mapPath` when no map is embedded, and still keeps the item verbatim as the `__displacePsd` template.
- `template()` accepts a template with either a map or a path. `export_item` accepts `mapPath` only when it equals the template's own `DspF`, so an unedited filter writes back byte-identical; a changed path still errors as before.
- A Mac alias (`alis`), non-`txtu`, truncated or empty path stays opaque, as before.

## Tests

- Unit: `a_map_named_only_by_its_path_imports_as_map_path` (import, byte-identical round trip, changed path refused, bad paths stay opaque).
- Regression: `displace_psd_filter_with_only_a_map_path_renders_after_replace_contents` in `crates/engine/tests/it/smart_psd.rs`, at 8, 16 and 32 bit: a synthetic PSD with a path-only Displace pointing at a temp PNG map, re-imported, then `replaceContents`; asserts no warnings and a displaced cache. Before the fix it fails with `the Displace... smart filter is not supported, so it was not applied`.

Ran (rustc 1.95): `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p photocraft-io -p photocraft-engine --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test -p photocraft-io`, the engine integration tests (incl. `panic_hunt`), `cargo xtask layers`, `cargo xtask wasm`, and the corpus set (`--features corpus,heif` on psd, codecs, io, engine): all pass. Re-ran the displace tests after rebasing on current `main`.

## Notes

- I could not check the reporter's file. If it does carry a `DspD` that still fails, this is a different cause and the file is needed.
- Not covered: Mac `alis` paths are still not decoded; an unreadable map file on re-render still passes pixels through silently (existing `resolve_map_path` behaviour).
- Unrelated: on Windows the `photocraft-engine` lib test binary crashed twice with `STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION` when run in parallel; with `--test-threads=1` all 2178 tests pass. This change touches no engine library code.

prs.title: raw: faster tone stage (Shadows, Highlights, Clarity, Texture, Dehaze), same bytes
prs.body:
Part of #9435 (F8, the tone stage).

With Shadows, Highlights, Clarity, Texture or Dehaze set, the full-size part of the raw develop cost as much as the whole AHD development at 45 MP (one slider: +26 G instructions on a 13.6 G bilinear develop; Texture +58 G). This change speeds that stage up without changing a single output byte. Only `crates/raw/src/tone.rs` is touched.

What it does, all with the same arithmetic in the same order:
- The bilinear lookup that carries the change maps (and Dehaze's transmission) to full size worked out the source position with divisions for every pixel, twice (plane `a` and plane `b`). The taps of every column and row are now computed once per image, and `a`/`b` are stored together.
- Texture's Gaussian bases ran the column pass down strided columns, one tap at a time with a mirror per tap. Both passes now accumulate neighbouring samples side by side, tap by tap in the old order.
- The box mean's column pass runs row-wise in blocks, the running sums per column unchanged.
- The luminance of the work copy and of Texture's copy is reduced in one pass over the pixels (each cell sums in the old order), and the work copy is skipped when only Texture is set and there is no black point.
- `log2` of the luminance is taken once for both changes.

Not changed (would change rounding): the per-pixel `log2f`/`exp2f` and the divisions of Dehaze.

## Proof of identical output
- Unit tests keep the replaced code (`bilinear_ref`, `gauss_ref`, `box_mean_ref`, `reduce`) and compare to_bits: odd sizes, kernels wider than the image, all sigmas/radii used.

prs.title: Startup: a failed launch says why in a dialog instead of closing silently (#7643)
prs.body:
Fixes #7643.

A launch that fails before the event loop starts exits through the `Err` from `eframe::run_native`, and a desktop launch has no console — release builds are GUI-subsystem on Windows, and a Dock/`open` launch has no terminal on macOS — so the error went nowhere and the app "just closed". The error wasn't logged either, so a reporter had nothing to attach.

`apps/photocraft/src/startup_report.rs` logs it and, when nothing else can see the failure, shows one native dialog (`rfd::MessageDialog`, the crate already used for the file dialogs):

```
PhotoCraft could not start.

wgpu error: No suitable GPU adapters found on the system!

Renderer: dx12
Startup: the previous start didn't finish on vulkan; using dx12
Version: 0.15.1 (3f2a9c1d0, 2026-10-01)
Log file: C:\Users\me\AppData\Roaming\Photocraft\logs\photocraft.log
```

The dialog is skipped when a launch can report the failure some other way, so nothing that worked before changes:

- **A terminal launch** (stderr is a terminal) keeps printing to stderr and exits: `cargo run` and the test harnesses never get a modal box.
- **A `--control` launch** is driven by an automation client that reads the exit status, so it stays silent too.
- **A headless Linux launch** (no `DISPLAY`, no `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` — the `startup_without_display` test removes both) has nowhere to put a dialog, so it keeps the error on stderr.

The `Log file:` line is left out when the logger never opened one (`--version`, a settings directory it can't write), and `Startup:` appears only when the renderer wasn't simply the preference — the crash-fallback case, where the app picks a backend the user never chose.

The body is English diagnostics like Help › System Info, so a bug report reads the same in every language; only the title goes through `i18n`.

`AppLogger` now remembers the file `attach_dir` opened (`path()`): after the fact the logger only held the `File`, and the dialog has to name the file a reporter should attach.

The CPU-retry path is unchanged: the parent hands off to `--safe-gpu` and returns before this, so the child reports its own failure.

## Tests

- `logging::tests::path_names_the_attached_log_file` — `None` before a file is attached, then the path `attach_dir` returned.
- `startup_report::tests::a_desktop_launch_asks_the_user_and_a_script_does_not` — the gate: desktop → dialog; a terminal, an automation client or no display → none.
- `startup_report::tests::the_text_names_the_error_renderer_version_and_log` — error, renderer, version and log path are in the text; no log line without a file; no `Startup:` line without a fallback.
- `startup_report::tests::a_fallback_that_was_not_the_preference_is_explained` — the fallback reason lands under the renderer.

Checks: `rustfmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p photocraft --all-targets --features heif -- -D warnings`, `cargo test -p photocraft --lib --bins`.

`docs/development.md` › Logs says the dialog exists, since that paragraph is what tells users which file to attach.

prs.title: Color Lookup: honour the .3dl Mesh header's cube edge and output depth (#9078, #9073)
prs.body:
## What

`parse_3dl` skipped every text line, so it ignored the Lustre `3DMESH` / `Mesh <inBits> <outBits>` header and inferred both the cube edge and the output code range from the data. The header declares the cube edge (2^inBits + 1) and the output range (up to 2^outBits − 1), and Photoshop honours both:

- **#9078**: a 3³ cube whose shaper line has exactly three values (`Mesh 1 12` + `0 512 1023` + 27 nodes) had its shaper counted as a 28th node → `28 rows is not a cube`, whole file rejected. With the header, the declared cube settles the ambiguity: one row too many whose first row has `n` values means that row is the shaper. Node-only tables (the reporter's positive control) are untouched.
- **#9073**: identical node bytes under `Mesh 2 10` vs `Mesh 2 12` must render differently (white → 255 vs grey 64, measured in Photoshop 27.11). The declaration now wins while it covers the data; a node beyond the declared range is treated as a wrong declaration and keeps the old max-value inference, so no file that loaded before stops loading.

Malformed or out-of-range `Mesh` values are ignored as before; a `Mesh` header that disagrees with the row count is refused with a clear error. Headerless `.3dl` behaviour is unchanged.

## Tests

- `three_dl_mesh_three_point_shaper_is_not_a_node` — the #9078 repro shape (3³, three-value shaper, 12-bit inverse nodes) parses; the shaper-less 27-node control parses identically.
- `three_dl_mesh_declares_the_output_depth` — the #9073 pair: same bytes, `Mesh 2 10` vs `Mesh 2 12`, corner divides by 1023 vs 4095.
- `three_dl_mesh_header_mismatch_is_rejected` — mismatch refused; over-range declaration falls back to inference.
- `color_lookup_mesh_3dl_honours_the_header` (engine) — end-to-end `image.adjustments.colorLookup` on the #9078 file: (64,128,192) renders (191,127,63) ±1, Photoshop's measured result.

Verified locally: `cargo test -p photocraft-cms`, `cargo test -p photocraft-engine --lib` (2187 passed), `cargo test -p photocraft-io --lib`, `cargo clippy -p photocraft-cms -p photocraft-engine --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo xtask layers`, `panic_hunt --ignored`. The change is pure std Rust (no platform code), so wasm is unaffected.

Fixes #9078
Fixes #9073

- `parse_3dl` now honours the `Mesh <inBits> <outBits>` line. A declaration is exactly two integers after the keyword, with `inBits` 1 to 7 and `outBits` 1 to 16; anything else (a non-number, too few or too many fields, out of range) is ignored as every text line was before, so such a file still loads by inference.

Any other count is an error naming the expected and found rows. The output scale is `2^outBits - 1`, also for a small maximum, and only when a node exceeds that range does the old inference apply, so a wrong declaration keeps loading as before.
- Without a declaration the old rule remains (edge from the cube root of the row count, scale inferred) in a helper, `inferred_3dl_scale`, which keeps the header rule that a headerless table peaking at 255 or 1023 is on the 12-bit scale. A `3DMESH` line with no numbers still counts as a header. The test that used `Mesh 1 10` to mean a header is changed to the bare magic, since that line now declares a 3³ cube.

prs.title: Affinity reader: contiguous curve records and a cheaper object tag index
prs.body:
Part of #9413

## What

- `stream.rs`: a fixed-size record array (`0x2c`, curve nodes) became one `Vec<Value::Bytes>` entry per record. It is now one `Value::Records { size, data }` buffer. Each record still counts as one value against `MAX_VALUES`, so the limit is unchanged. `geometry::curves` reads the nodes straight from the buffer; `Value::array_len` gives the slot count for both array kinds, and the other readers of array fields (slot charging in `access.rs`, gradient positions in `paint.rs`, column widths in `text.rs`) treat the new variant like the array of byte values it replaces. Records of a width other than 18 are still no curve nodes.
- `stream.rs`: the per-object SipHash `HashMap<Tag, usize>` is gone. Objects with up to 12 fields are scanned; larger ones use a sorted `(tag, first index)` table with a binary search (still logarithmic, so many-field hostile objects cannot go quadratic; no unseeded fast hasher because tags come from the file). First-match semantics and tag 0 handling are unchanged.
- `model.rs`: `read()` drops the inflated `doc.dat` once the stream is parsed.

`stream::Value` is public and gets a new variant; nothing else in the workspace matches on it.

## Proof of identical output

- A hash of the whole parsed `Document` (all metadata plus raw pixel bytes) equals main on 7 large synthetic documents and on all 39 files of the public corpus.
- A test keeps the old per-object map and compares `Object::get` for every object size 0..59 with repeated and positional tags. Another checks the record array layout and `array_len`.

## Measurements

`perf stat`, one pinned core, main and branch alternated, 5 rounds, medians; peak RSS from a single run.

| Document | Instructions | Cycles | Peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2000 curves x 2000 nodes (100 MB) | 2.11e10 -> 1.15e10 (-46%) | 6.04e9 -> 3.83e9 | 1136 -> 531 MB |
| 50 000 shapes | 3.17e9 -> 2.38e9 (-25%) | 1.27e9 -> 0.82e9 | 174 -> 127 MB |
| 2000 text layers | 9.8e8 -> 8.6e8 (-12%) | 2.8e8 -> 2.2e8 | 51 -> 38 MB |

Dropping `doc.dat` early alone is worth about 63 MB of peak on the curve document. The real corpus is tiny (all 39 files read in about 50 ms in total), so the gain shows on the large synthetic documents.

Left out because no gain was measured here: `objs()` returning an iterator, the `Vec<char>` text path, the tile-cache retention in `plane()`.

Checks: `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy -p photocraft-affinity --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --release -p photocraft-affinity`, `cargo check -p photocraft-io`.

prs.title: fix(format): a save on macOS keeps the file's creation time (#9388)
prs.body:
Fixes #9388.

On macOS, saving over an existing file reset its creation date ("Created" in Finder) to the time of the save. Save writes a temporary file and renames it over the original (`crates/format/src/atomic.rs`), so the renamed file is a new inode born at the save. The issue asked for someone with a Mac to check; this was checked on macOS 27.2 (Apple silicon).

### Photoshop's behaviour

Photoshop 2025 (26.2) on macOS, by script: save a synthetic 32×32 document as a PSD, wait four seconds, change it and save again. `stat` before and after:

| | created | modified |
|---|---|---|
| after the first save | 04:10:59 | 04:10:59 |
| after the re-save | **04:10:59** (kept) | 04:11:04 |

### What changes

- `atomic::meta::copy_metadata` gains a macOS step, `copy_created`. It reads the replaced file's creation time and sets it on the temporary file, using `std::os::macos::fs::FileTimesExt::set_created` and `File::set_times` (stable since Rust 1.75), before the rename. The rename keeps it.
- Like the other metadata steps, it's best effort and never touches the bytes.
- The module's table now lists macOS creation time as carried over. The comment saying it needed an unsafe `setattrlist` is gone.

### Verification

`photocraft-cli run --new … --out f.psd`, wait three seconds, then `photocraft-cli run f.psd --cmd edit.fill … --out f.psd --in-place`:

| | created after the re-save | modified after the re-save | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | moved to the save time (04:10:38 → 04:10:51) | save time | – |
| this PR | kept (04:16:26 → 04:16:26) | save time (04:16:29) | created kept, modified updated |

### Tests

- `atomic::tests::keeps_the_original_creation_time` (macOS only): a file whose creation time is set well in the past keeps it through `atomic_write`, the new bytes are in place, and no temporary file is left. It fails with the step disabled.
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for format; `cargo test -p photocraft-format` (68 + 100); `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`. All pass.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

It is set before the ACL is copied, because a copied ACL that denies its owner write access would refuse the open; the error joins the existing attributes/ACL/permissions result. The automation write path (`workspace.rs`) does the same through its already-open handles with the new `copy_created_file`, ignoring a failure there. prs.title: fix(io, engine): Embed Color Profile writes sRGB for an untagged document (#9325)
prs.body:
Fixes #9325.

A JPEG exported from a new document had no colour profile, even with Export As › Embed Color Profile on. New documents in the default working space are untagged: `icc_profile: None`, which PhotoCraft treats as sRGB (its Dot Gain 20 %-compatible working gray for grayscale). The exporters only embedded a profile the document carried, so viewers and online platforms had to guess.

### Photoshop's behaviour

Photoshop 2025 (26.2) on macOS, by script: a 64×64 synthetic document filled with one colour.
- **Save As JPEG** with Embed Color Profile.
- **Save for Web** with JPEG and Include Profile.

The embedded profile was read back from each file:

| Document | Save As JPEG | Save for Web JPEG |
|---|---|---|
| new (Working RGB: sRGB) | sRGB IEC61966-2.1 | sRGB IEC61966-2.1 |
| set to Don't Color Manage | sRGB IEC61966-2.1 | sRGB IEC61966-2.1 |

### What changes

- **io** (`flat::export_flat_with`): an untagged image gets the profile assumed for its mode when the target format can carry one. That's built-in sRGB for RGB, and for gray the Dot Gain 20 %-compatible working gray the canvas shows it through (not sGray, which would look darker). This covers Export As, Save As / Save a Copy and the CLI.
  - The codec still leaves the profile out when `embed_icc` is off.
  - Formats that can't hold a profile take the existing path unchanged, so they get no new "profile dropped" warning.
  - The CMYK branch already writes the built-in Coated CMYK for an untagged CMYK target, so this follows the same rule.
- **engine** (Save for Web): with Embed Color Profile on, an untagged document's file carries sRGB. `web_document` already treats such documents "as sRGB already". With it off, nothing changes.

### Verification

Same steps on main and this branch: `photocraft-cli run --new … --cmd edit.fill --out new.jpg|png|webp`.

| | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| untagged RGB → JPEG | no profile | sRGB (built-in) | sRGB IEC61966-2.1 |
| untagged RGB → PNG / WebP | no profile | `iCCP` / `ICCP` sRGB | – |
| Embed Color Profile off | no profile | no profile | – |
| tagged (Display P3) | Display P3 | Display P3 | – |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- **Every flat export of an untagged document now carries sRGB/sGray when embedding is on.** That includes the CLI's `run --out`, so files grow by PhotoCraft's built-in profile (about 650 bytes). Photoshop does the same for new documents.
- **Four tests relied on untagged exports having no profile.** Each now asks for that explicitly:
  - `color_cmds::exif_srgb_jpeg_round_trip`: the EXIF ColorSpace path needs a file without ICC.
  - `export_dialog::the_estimate_is_the_exported_files_size`: its premise measures the proxy's pixel error. A fixed-size profile scaled with the pixels blurred that, so the test now runs with `embedProfile: false`.
  - The Affinity preview fixture in `engine/tests/it/affinity.rs`: Affinity previews carry no profile, and the hardened preview reader refuses compressed PNG chunks.
  - `automation::rpc::doc_save_rejects_a_bad_quality…`: a WebP with a profile is the extended `VP8X` layout, so the test looks for the lossy `VP8 ` chunk anywhere rather than at byte 12.
- The Export As size estimate scales the proxy's whole file, profile included. That was already true for tagged documents. The error is about 650 bytes × the scale ratio, and the exact estimate covers sizes up to `EXACT_ESTIMATE_PX`.

### Tests

- `flat::assumed_profile_tests::untagged_documents_embed_the_profile_they_are_assumed_to_be_in` covers:
  - JPEG, PNG, TIFF and WebP of an untagged RGB document carry sRGB;
  - a gray PNG carries the Dot Gain 20 %-compatible working gray;
  - with embedding off, there's none;
  - a BMP gets no profile warning;
  - a Display P3 document keeps P3.
- `web_cmds::tests::embed_color_profile_tags_an_untagged_document_srgb` covers Save for Web JPEG and PNG-24, with the option on and off.
- Both fail without their change.
- `cargo fmt --check`; clippy `-D warnings` for io, engine, ui-egui and automation; `cargo test` for io, engine (2187 + 277), ui-egui (3798 + 132), automation and cli; the rest of the workspace; `cargo xtask test-corpus` (4733 passed); `cargo xtask layers`; `cargo xtask wasm`. All pass.

prs.title: fix(export): embed requested sRGB profile for untagged sources (#9325)
prs.body:
Fixes #9325.

Export As already offers Convert to sRGB and Embed Color Profile, but skipped conversion for inputs without ICC data. Honor the requested sRGB destination using the **effective source profile from the original session**: a valid embedded profile takes precedence, otherwise use that session’s working profile.

Capture the profile for save callbacks, selected-layer batches, preview workers and exact-size workers. Pin it onto the export copy before conversion; RGB sources whose profile is byte-identical to sRGB retain their pixel tiles. Other sources use the existing colour converter. Preview cache signatures include the source-profile hash so working-space changes invalidate an untagged preview without requiring a document edit.

## Validation

- Full UI suite: **3,935 passed, 20 ignored**; all-target UI Clippy, formatting, dependency layers and WASM passed. The dense 24 MP tile-reuse check was run separately and passed.
- The new app replay regression fails on the previous head: Policy Off + untagged Display P3 pixels were merely labelled sRGB. It now checks Display P3 and Adobe RGB at 8/16/32-bit against a tagged conversion control, requires a real pixel change, and verifies source immutability.
- UI cache tests verify working-profile changes without document revision, and embedded-profile precedence. Removing the profile hash makes the cache regression fail. Native workers retain the captured profile even if the original session changes afterwards.
- Existing real JPEG encode/import tests cover RGB 8/16/32-bit, Gray and CMYK, embedding opt-out, and Document Profile. Native offscreen inspection of the P3 export preview was also performed.

The existing control screenshot below is UI context; ICC and converted pixel behavior are verified by tests.

![Export As controls](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vanvo/photocraft/9082d388bcf3fbecea1b649b771582f77f3f5d98/export-options.png)

[Screenshot attribution and licenses](https://github.com/vanvo/photocraft/blob/9082d388bcf3fbecea1b649b771582f77f3f5d98/ATTRIBUTION.md).

prs.title: feat(ui): Preset menus for Levels, Exposure, Black & White and Channel Mixer
prs.body:
Fixes #9263, fixes #9265, fixes #9268, fixes #9270.

Levels, Exposure, Black & White and Channel Mixer gain a **Preset** menu at the top of their editor (Image › Adjustments dialog and the adjustment layer's Properties), as in Photoshop. It lists the preset names Photoshop uses and reads **Custom** once the settings are edited. Choosing a preset is one edit, which the preview follows.

### The settings are original

**These presets' settings are PhotoCraft's own.** Each was designed for the look its name describes. None was copied, measured or read from Photoshop's (or any other application's) preset files, and the clean-room rule in AGENTS.md was followed. Only the names, which describe the looks, follow Photoshop's menus.

- **Levels:**
  - Darker lowers the white output; Lighter brings the white input in.
  - Increase Contrast 1/2/3 pull both input points in, further each step.
  - Lighten Shadows lifts the black output and opens the gamma a little.
  - Midtones Brighter/Darker move the gamma only.
- **Exposure:** Minus/Plus 1.0 and 2.0 are whole stops.
- **Black & White:** the filter presets follow what a coloured lens filter does on black-and-white film: it lightens its own colour and darkens its complement.
  - Red: dark skies. Blue: light skies, dark skin tones.
  - The High Contrast variants push further.
  - Infrared makes foliage glow and skies go dark.
  - Maximum Black and Maximum White take every colour to the ends.
  - Neutral Density weighs every colour the same.
- **Channel Mixer:** monochrome mixes of the channels each filter would let through: a red filter is the red channel, orange is half red and half green, infrared is mostly green.

The tables are in `crates/ui-egui/src/adjust_presets.rs`, with this note at the top of the file and one comment per preset.

### What changes

- `adjust_presets.rs` (new): the preset tables and `presets(kind, gray)`.
  - `settings` gives a preset over the kind's defaults, as the engine normalises it.
  - `matching` finds which preset the current settings are, or Custom.
- `adjust_editors::editor` draws a `Preset:` row above these four editors through the common dispatcher, so the dialog and Properties both get it.
  - Levels shows it in RGB and Grayscale documents.
  - Black & White and Channel Mixer show it only in colour documents.
- `docs/ui-parity.md`: revision.

### Verification

A synthetic chart (a grey ramp over a hue/brightness sweep) run through the presets with the CLI:
- Each Black & White and Channel Mixer filter brightens its own band and darkens the complement.
- Infrared whitens the greens and yellows and blackens the blues; Neutral Density is flat.
- Increase Contrast 3, Lighten Shadows, Midtones Darker and Darker change the tones as named.

| Adjustment | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Levels / Exposure / Black & White / Channel Mixer | no Preset menu | Preset menu (these names, Custom after an edit) | Preset menu with these names (its settings weren't used) |

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- **One shared module** serves all four kinds, wired through the common editor dispatcher. My separate Curves presets PR (#9234) has its own module, and #9251 (another contributor) covers Hue/Saturation. These could be folded into this one later.
- **The menu is UI-only.** Scripts and agents set the values directly.
- **The preset values are a design choice**, kept in one table each, and are easy to tune.

### Tests

- `adjust_presets::tests::presets_apply_and_are_recognised`:
  - Every preset is valid, distinct and recognised after it's applied; untouched settings read Default; an edit reads Custom.
  - Colour presets aren't offered in Grayscale.
- `adjust_presets::tests::presets_give_their_looks`:
  - Contrast steps widen and gamma presets point the right way.
  - Filters lighten their own colour over the complement, and the High Contrast red filter goes further.
  - Exposure stops are exact, and the Channel Mixer presets are monochrome.
- `adjust_dialog::tests::adjustment_preset_menus_load_presets_and_read_custom_after_an_edit` (UI harness, real menu clicks in all four dialogs):
  - Each opens on Default, loads the chosen preset, and reads Custom after an edit.
  - It fails without the Preset row.
- The 106 existing adjustment editor tests pass unchanged. `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p photocraft-ui-egui --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test -p photocraft-ui-egui` (3799 + 132 passed), `cargo xtask layers` and `cargo xtask wasm` pass.

prs.title: Gradient Fill layer: default to Foreground to Transparent (#8708)
prs.body:
Fixes #8708.

A new Gradient Fill layer (Layer › New Fill Layer › Gradient…, or the Layers panel's fill button) was an opaque gradient from the foreground to the background colour. With the default white background it covered the layers below with white at one end, which is what the report calls "a solid white background instead of transparency".

### Anything a reviewer should look at first

- **The target is Photoshop's Foreground to Transparent.** In Photoshop 2025 (26.2) on this Mac, Layer › New Fill Layer › Gradient… opens with the foreground fading to transparent (Linear, 90°). Photoshop remembers that dialog's last gradient, and I couldn't rule out that this is a remembered choice without resetting Photoshop's preferences, which I didn't do. I'm taking it as the default because it's the closest case I observed, and it's what the reporter expects.
- **How it's built:** the foreground at both colour stops plus transparency stops 100% → 0% (`opacity_stops`), the same shape a PSD stores for Photoshop's Foreground to Transparent. An explicit `to` keeps the old two-colour gradient, so scripts that pass both colours don't change.

### What changes

- `crates/engine/src/commands.rs` (`layer.newFillLayer.gradient`): with no `to`, colour stops `from`/`from` plus transparency stops `(0, 100%)`, `(1, 0%)`. The params doc says so.
- New test `gradient_fill_cmds::tests::new_gradient_fill_layer_defaults_to_foreground_to_transparent`.

### Tests

- The new test checks the default stops, and that a `to` colour still gives a two-colour gradient with no transparency stops. It fails on main (the second stop is the background colour) and passes with the fix.
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p photocraft-engine --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test -p photocraft-engine --lib --tests` (2184 + 277 and the rest passed), `panic_hunt` (`--ignored`), `cargo xtask layers` and `cargo xtask wasm` pass.

### Verification

A 200×100 transparent document, foreground (51, 102, 153), background white, a new Gradient Fill layer with the defaults. Pixel at x = 100, from the top (y = 0, 25, 50, 75, 99):

| | main | this PR | Photoshop 2025 (Foreground to Transparent, Linear 90°) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Colour | white → (53, 104, 154) | (51, 102, 153) throughout | (51, 102, 153) throughout |
| Alpha | 255 everywhere | 0, 64, 128, 191, 252 | 0, 52, 128, 203, 254 |

The difference in alpha at the quarter points comes from Photoshop's "Smooth" gradient method, which eases the ramp. PhotoCraft's gradient fills are linear for every gradient, two-colour ones too, so that's a separate change and not part of this PR.
